title: What Counts as a Religion
description: Definitions, categories, and the scholar's stance toward belief

concepts.title: Three Classic Definitions
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask scholars of religion what their subject is and you won't get one answer, because they have no agreed definition. Three classic attempts still frame the debate. In Primitive Culture (1871) the English anthropologist Edward Burnett Tylor proposed a "minimum definition" of religion as "the belief in Spiritual Beings." His theory of animism treated religion as an early attempt to explain dreams, death and the living world.

The French sociologist Émile Durkheim, in The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912), moved the focus from beings to community. Religion, he wrote, is "a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things, that is to say, things set apart and forbidden,"1 which unite adherents into "one single moral community." He built the case on Aboriginal Australian totemism, though he never visited Australia and relied on ethnographers' reports. In 1966 the American anthropologist Clifford Geertz called religion "a system of symbols" that creates powerful, lasting moods and motivations by picturing a general order of existence and making that picture seem uniquely real. Talal Asad later objected that Geertz's stress on inner meaning universalized a modern, Protestant-shaped idea of religion.

Between them, these attempts show a basic split. Substantive definitions say what religion is by its content, meaning gods, spirits, the supernatural. Functional definitions say what religion does, such as binding groups, giving meaning, or expressing what Paul Tillich called "ultimate concern." Definitions centered on God don't fit forms of Buddhism and Jainism well, since both reject a creator god, while functional ones can sweep in nationalism or devoted sports fandom. Many scholars now prefer a family-resemblance approach, such as Ninian Smart's dimensions of religion: ritual, narrative, experience, ethics, doctrine, social organization and, in later versions, material culture.

concepts.title: The World Religions Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Open a textbook on religion and you'll often find a list of large traditions (usually Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity and Islam, often with Sikhism, Confucianism, Daoism and Shinto), each treated as a bounded system with scriptures and a creed. Many textbooks are still organized this way, under the world religions paradigm. In The Invention of World Religions (2005), Tomoko Masuzawa traced how this list took shape in nineteenth- and early twentieth-century European scholarship. She argued that it carried a hidden hierarchy. Christianity served as the model of what a religion is, other traditions were measured against it, and "universal" religions were ranked above "national" or "primitive" ones.

The model fits some traditions badly. Whether Confucianism is a religion has been argued for centuries. In the Chinese Rites controversy, Jesuit missionaries held that rites honoring Confucius and ancestors were civil, not religious, so converts could keep them; Rome banned the rites in 1715 and lifted the ban in 1939. Japanese didn't have an exact equivalent of "religion," and shūkyō settled in as the translation only in the 1870s and 1880s. The Meiji state came to class shrine Shinto as civic ritual rather than religion, which let it expect shrine observance while promising religious freedom in the 1889 constitution.

Many Indigenous traditions likewise lack a separate word for religion, because ceremony, kinship, land, law and healing depend on one another. Forcing them into the box can distort them, yet legal protection often depends on it. Wilfred Cantwell Smith argued in 1962 that "religion" as a self-contained system is a modern Western notion, and Jonathan Z. Smith wrote in 1982 that "religion is solely the creation of the scholar's study." Most scholars still use the word, treating it as a tool for examining traditions.

concepts.title: Insiders, Outsiders, and Methodological Agnosticism
concepts.contentHtml:
The academic study of religion is often traced to Friedrich Max Müller, a German-born Oxford philologist who called in the 1870s for a "science of religion" built on comparison. Adapting a line of Goethe's about languages, he declared of religions: "He who knows one, knows none." Anyone who compares religions soon has to ask whose description counts.

Scholars borrowed a pair of terms coined by the linguist Kenneth Pike in 1954.1 An emic account uses the categories meaningful to participants, such as a Hindu speaking of darśan, the exchange of sight between deity and worshipper. An etic account uses the observer's comparative categories, such as "image veneration." Neither's simply right. Insiders know things outsiders miss, but insiders disagree with one another, and their accounts are themselves evidence to study. Outsiders can compare across traditions but may impose alien frames. Scholars of religion include believers of many kinds and nonbelievers, and the field asks all of them to argue from evidence open to anyone.

The working rule is methodological agnosticism, a phrase associated with Ninian Smart. The scholar brackets whether a religion's claims are true and studies what people believe, do and experience. Peter Berger had earlier used "methodological atheism" for a similar stance in sociology, a label critics thought implied a verdict. Phenomenologists of religion called this bracketing epoché. Bracketing doesn't endorse or dismiss belief, and it leaves questions of truth to theology and the philosophy of religion, which pursue them by their own methods.

title: Myth and Sacred Story
description: How scholars read myths, test comparisons, and trace how scriptures became fixed

concepts.title: Myth Is Not a Synonym for False
concepts.contentHtml:
In everyday speech a "myth" is a falsehood. Scholars use the word differently: a myth is a traditional narrative, usually about origins, gods, ancestors or the end of things, that carries authority for a community. Calling the Genesis creation account or the Vedic hymn of the cosmic person (Purusha Sukta) a myth makes no judgment about its truth; it names the kind of work the story does. Greek mythos first meant simply "word" or "story" and only later came to be contrasted with logos, a reasoned account.

Theories differ on what that work is. Bronisław Malinowski, drawing on fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands, called myth a "charter" (1926): a story that justifies present institutions, such as which group holds which land. Bruce Lincoln (1999) called myth "ideology in narrative form," adding that scholarship is "myth with footnotes." Mircea Eliade (1907 to 1986), the Romanian-born historian of religions who taught at the University of Chicago, read myth as an account of what happened in the sacred time of beginnings, in illo tempore. For Eliade the sacred breaks into ordinary space in a hierophany,1 and rituals re-enact mythic events so that participants return to that time.

Eliade's broad patterns, such as the axis mundi or world center, dominated the field from the 1950s into the 1980s. Critics, including Jonathan Z. Smith, argued that he lifted examples out of their historical settings and assumed a universal "religious man" (homo religiosus) that the evidence did not establish. Others charged that his idea of the sacred carried theology into supposedly neutral comparison, a charge his defenders dispute.

concepts.title: Structures and Patterns: Lévi-Strauss and the Dying God
concepts.contentHtml:
The French anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss took a different route in "The Structural Study of Myth" (1955) and the four volumes of Mythologiques (1964 to 1971). Borrowing from structural linguistics, he argued that a myth's meaning lies not in its plot but in relations among its units, which he called mythemes,1 and above all in binary oppositions such as raw and cooked, nature and culture, life and death. Myth, he wrote, provides "a logical model capable of overcoming a contradiction." Because meaning lies in structure, a myth is the sum of all its versions; he even counted Freud's reading of Oedipus as one more version of the Oedipus myth. Critics replied that the oppositions are often the analyst's rather than the storytellers', and that the method is hard to test.

An older comparative project shows the risks. In The Golden Bough (first edition 1890), James George Frazer grouped Adonis, Attis, Osiris and the Mesopotamian Tammuz (Sumerian Dumuzi) as dying-and-rising gods whose yearly death and return mirrored the crops. Later writers used the pattern to argue that the Christian resurrection story was borrowed, a claim most historians of antiquity regard as overstated.

In a 1987 encyclopedia article, Jonathan Z. Smith argued that the category was largely a scholarly construction resting on late, fragmentary or ambiguous sources. Osiris does not return to earthly life but reigns among the dead, and the evidence for Adonis rising comes from late texts. Tryggve Mettinger (2001) answered that some figures, such as Dumuzi and the Ugaritic Baal, do fit a pattern of death and return, while agreeing that this does not show the Gospels copied them. Most specialists now use the category cautiously, if at all.

concepts.title: Floods, Borrowing, and the Making of Canons
concepts.contentHtml:
Flood stories show comparison at its most solid. In 1872 George Smith of the British Museum announced that a cuneiform tablet from Nineveh,1 part of what is now Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, told of a man warned by a god to build a boat, who survived a deluge and sent out birds to find land. An older Mesopotamian version, the Atrahasis epic, survives in copies from around the seventeenth century BCE. The detailed parallels with Genesis 6 to 9 lead most biblical scholars to conclude that the Genesis account draws, directly or indirectly, on Mesopotamian tradition. That is a claim about contact between texts, resting on dated manuscripts.

Claims about flood stories worldwide are weaker. Stories from Greece (Deucalion), India (Manu warned by a fish) and the Americas vary widely; some recorded after missionary contact may echo the Bible; and geology shows no single global flood. Explanations range from diffusion to the shared experience of river floods. The idea that one prehistoric event, such as a sudden flooding of the Black Sea, lies behind them remains contested.

Sacred texts also have histories of selection. A canon (Greek kanōn, "measuring rod") is a closed list of authoritative writings. The earliest surviving list matching the 27 books of the New Testament appears in a letter by Athanasius of Alexandria in 367 CE. Muslim tradition holds that a standard text of the Qur'an was fixed under the caliph Uthman (ruled 644 to 656). The Pali Canon of Theravada Buddhism was passed on orally before being written down in Sri Lanka, traditionally in the first century BCE.

title: Ritual and Practice
description: Rites of passage, theories of sacrifice, pilgrimage, and the turn to lived religion

concepts.title: Rites of Passage and Liminality
concepts.contentHtml:
In Les Rites de passage (1909) the French ethnographer Arnold van Gennep observed that ceremonies marking birth, initiation, marriage and death in many societies share a three-part structure:1 separation from a former status, a transition or margin, and incorporation into a new one. He called the middle phase liminal, from Latin limen, "threshold." A baptism, a bar mitzvah, a graduation or the funeral rites that turn a dead person into an ancestor can all be read through this pattern.

The British anthropologist Victor Turner made the middle phase his subject. Working among the Ndembu of what is now Zambia in the 1950s,2 he described boys in circumcision rites as "betwixt and between" (The Forest of Symbols, 1967): stripped of names and rank, treated as both dead and newborn, set outside ordinary social order. In The Ritual Process (1969) he argued that liminality produces communitas, an intense, egalitarian bond among those who share the threshold, standing against the hierarchy of everyday "structure." He later called the optional, leisure-time versions found in modern societies, such as festivals and the arts, "liminoid."

The model's strength is a portable vocabulary for comparison. Its weakness, critics say, is that it treats rituals as texts awaiting the scholar's decoding. Catherine Bell (1992) argued instead for studying "ritualization," the strategic ways people set certain acts apart and thereby produce authority and social distinctions. Many rituals mark no passage at all, and participants do not always feel the transformation the theory predicts.

concepts.title: Theories of Sacrifice
concepts.contentHtml:
Sacrifice, the ritual offering and often killing of an animal or other gift, appears in ancient Israel, Vedic India, Greece, China and Mesoamerica, which made it a prize for grand theory. Tylor saw it as a gift to win divine favor; William Robertson Smith (1889) saw it as a communal meal shared with the god. In an essay of 1899, the French sociologists Henri Hubert and Marcel Mauss, working mainly from Vedic and Hebrew texts, argued that sacrifice opens communication between the sacred and profane worlds through a victim that is consecrated and destroyed. They distinguished the "sacrifier," who receives the benefit, from the "sacrificer," who performs the act.

Later theories sought deep origins. The classicist Walter Burkert, in Homo Necans (1972), traced Greek sacrifice to Paleolithic hunting: killing created anxiety and guilt, and ritual managed them, for instance by staging the animal's apparent consent. The literary theorist René Girard, in Violence and the Sacred (1972), proposed that imitative ("mimetic") desire breeds rivalry that threatens to engulf a community until violence converges on a single scapegoat; sacrifice repeats that founding violence in controlled form. Girard, a Catholic, later argued that the Gospels expose the mechanism by presenting the victim as innocent.

These remain theories, not established findings. In the 1987 volume Violent Origins, Jonathan Z. Smith countered the hunting hypothesis by noting that sacrificial victims are overwhelmingly domesticated animals, which ties sacrifice to herding and farming societies, and he doubted that any single origin story could explain it. Other critics note that one-cause theories flatten traditions in which sacrifice means very different things, and that Girard's thesis is hard to test against evidence.

concepts.title: Pilgrimage and Lived Religion
concepts.contentHtml:
Pilgrimage puts ritual on the move. The Hajj to Mecca, one of the Five Pillars of Islam, is required once in a lifetime of every adult Muslim who is physically and financially able. Saudi Arabia limits numbers with national quotas; its statistics authority counted about 1.83 million pilgrims in 2024, against a peak of over 3 million in 2012. The Hindu Kumbh Mela rotates among four river sites. Uttar Pradesh officials announced over 660 million bathers at Prayagraj across 45 days in early 2025, an official estimate that cannot be independently checked and probably counts many people more than once. On the Camino de Santiago in Spain, the Pilgrim's Office issued nearly half a million certificates in 2024 to people who walked at least the final 100 km, many of whom describe their motives as partly or wholly non-religious.

Victor and Edith Turner (1978) read pilgrimage as liminal, a journey that produces communitas. John Eade and Michael Sallnow (1991) replied that shrines are arenas where pilgrims, clergy, locals and states contest the meaning of the sacred.

That exchange reflects a wider shift. Early scholarship, shaped by Protestant emphasis on scripture and inner faith, often treated belief and doctrine as the core of religion. From the 1980s and 1990s, studies of lived religion, such as Robert Orsi's The Madonna of 115th Street (1985) on an Italian American festa in East Harlem, turned to what people do: home altars, healing, food, festivals, prayer. They found that everyday practice often diverges from official teaching and that people mix sources freely.

title: Experience and Mysticism
description: Religious experience from William James to cognitive and evolutionary science

concepts.title: William James and the Varieties
concepts.contentHtml:
The American psychologist and philosopher William James gave the Gifford Lectures at Edinburgh in 1901 and 1902 and published them as The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902).1 He set institutions and theology aside and defined religion, for his purposes, as "the feelings, acts, and experiences of individual men in their solitude, so far as they apprehend themselves to stand in relation to whatever they may consider the divine." His evidence was mostly first-person testimony: diaries, autobiographies, letters and conversion narratives.

James contrasted the "healthy-minded," for whom faith comes easily, with the "sick soul," who must be "twice-born" through crisis and conversion. He proposed four marks of mystical states: ineffability (they defy description), a noetic quality (they feel like knowledge), transiency and passivity. Such states, he concluded, carry authority for the person who has them but impose no duty on others to accept their revelations uncritically. As a pragmatist he judged experiences by their fruits, not their roots: an experience is not discredited simply because it has a bodily or psychological cause.

A related line ran through German Protestant thought. Friedrich Schleiermacher (1799) placed religion in feeling rather than doctrine, and Rudolf Otto's The Idea of the Holy (1917) described the numinous, a mysterium tremendum et fascinans: a mystery that both terrifies and attracts. Later critics noted that this focus on private experience reflects a modern, largely Protestant picture of religion that can sideline ritual, community and law.

concepts.title: Perennialism Versus Constructivism
concepts.contentHtml:
A central debate asks whether mystics in different traditions encounter the same reality. Perennialists say yes, at least at the core. Aldous Huxley's The Perennial Philosophy (1945) gathered sayings from Christian, Hindu, Buddhist, Sufi and Daoist sources to argue for a shared insight beneath differing doctrines. The philosopher W. T. Stace, in Mysticism and Philosophy (1960), proposed a "common core": extrovertive mysticism, which sees unity in the world, and introvertive mysticism, an awareness of undifferentiated unity without content. On this view differences arise when mystics interpret the experience afterward in their tradition's vocabulary.

Constructivists reject the split between experience and interpretation. In a 1978 essay, "Language, Epistemology, and Mysticism," Steven Katz argued that "there are NO pure (i.e. unmediated) experiences." A Jewish kabbalist formed by divine names and commandments does not have the same experience as a Buddhist meditator trained to see the absence of a lasting self; training shapes the experience itself, not only the later report. Wayne Proudfoot (1985) added that people identify an experience as religious partly by explaining its cause in religious terms.

The argument continues. Robert Forman and others (1990) held that "pure consciousness events" in meditation, alert awareness with no content, show something constructivism cannot explain. Constructivists answer that such reports are shaped by the traditions that teach the practice. Ann Taves (2009) proposed setting aside what religious experience "really" is and studying how people come to deem some experiences religious or special.

concepts.title: Cognitive and Evolutionary Theories
concepts.contentHtml:
Since the 1990s the cognitive science of religion (CSR) has asked why religious ideas come so easily to human minds. Stewart Guthrie's Faces in the Clouds (1993) argued that people habitually see agents behind ambiguous events. The psychologist Justin Barrett named the proposed mechanism a hyperactive (or hypersensitive) agency detection device: mistaking wind for a predator costs little, while the reverse error can be fatal, so selection might favor false alarms. The anthropologist Pascal Boyer (Religion Explained, 2001) argued that successful religious ideas are minimally counterintuitive: a ghost is a person in nearly every respect but can pass through walls, which makes the idea memorable yet easy to reason with.

These are research programs with active critics. Memory experiments on such concepts have produced mixed results, and the theory struggles to explain why people worship some counterintuitive beings but not others, a puzzle nicknamed the "Mickey Mouse problem." CSR also tends to define religion, as Tylor did, by belief in supernatural agents, and many studies rely on narrow, mostly Western samples.

Evolutionary accounts divide. By-product theories (Boyer, Scott Atran) hold that religion rides on mental tools evolved for other jobs. Adaptationist theories hold that religion helped groups cooperate. Richard Sosis and Eric Bressler (2003) found that among 83 nineteenth-century American communes, religious ones tended to outlast secular ones. Ara Norenzayan's Big Gods (2013) ties moralizing gods to large-scale cooperation; a 2019 Nature paper arguing that complex societies came first was retracted in 2021 over its handling of missing data, and the question remains open. Explaining why a belief arises does not settle whether it is true, a point Barrett, himself a Christian, stresses.

title: Religion in the World Today
description: Secularization debates, a changing global map, and religion under law

concepts.title: The Secularization Debate
concepts.contentHtml:
Many founders of social science expected religion to fade with modernity. Max Weber spoke in 1917 of the "disenchantment of the world" by science and bureaucracy. By the 1960s the secularization thesis was close to orthodoxy in sociology, argued by Bryan Wilson (1966) and by Peter Berger, whose The Sacred Canopy (1967) described how pluralism erodes the taken-for-granted authority of any single faith. In 1968 Berger told the New York Times that by the twenty-first century religious believers were likely to be found "only in small sects, huddled together to resist a worldwide secular culture."

Berger changed his mind. Introducing The Desecularization of the World (1999), which he edited, he called the assumption that we live in a secularized world false and wrote that most of the world was "as furiously religious as it ever was." He later summed up that he had been wrong about secularization but right about pluralism. Rodney Stark's essay "Secularization, R.I.P." (1999) went further, arguing that religious markets with competing suppliers, as in the United States, keep participation high.

Others refined rather than buried the thesis. José Casanova (1994) separated three claims: the differentiation of religion from state, science and economy; the decline of belief and practice; and the privatization of religion. The first, he argued, is a real feature of modernity; the other two are not inevitable. Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart (2004) linked decline to existential security, so that safe, wealthy welfare states secularize fastest. Steve Bruce still defends the classic thesis for Western Europe, and Charles Taylor's A Secular Age (2007) recast secularity as a condition in which belief is one option among others.

concepts.title: A Changing Religious Map
concepts.contentHtml:
Global surveys show change in opposite directions at once. A Pew Research Center study published in 2025, covering 2010 to 2020, estimated about 2.3 billion Christians (just under 29 percent of humanity),1 about 2 billion Muslims and about 1.9 billion religiously unaffiliated people (about 24 percent). Muslims grew fastest, mainly because Muslim populations are younger and have higher fertility, not through conversion. Christians grew in number but fell as a share, largely because many people raised Christian in Western countries no longer identify with any religion. Sub-Saharan Africa overtook Europe as the region with the most Christians.

In some countries the unaffiliated are rising fast. In the 2021 census of England and Wales, 46.2 percent described themselves as Christian, the first time below half, and 37.2 percent reported no religion.2 In the United States, Pew's 2023 to 2024 survey found 62 percent identifying as Christian, down from 78 percent in 2007, though the share had held roughly steady since about 2019. Two cautions apply. These figures measure self-identification, not belief or practice. And "unaffiliated" does not mean atheist: many unaffiliated people pray, believe in God or spirits, or honor ancestors, as in China, where estimates of religious adherence vary enormously with the questions asked.

New groups keep appearing. Scholars use the neutral term new religious movements rather than "cult," a word that became strongly pejorative in the 1970s. Most such movements are small and peaceful, a few have been gravely harmful, and some, such as the Latter-day Saints (founded 1830), have grown into worldwide churches.

concepts.title: Religion and the Law
concepts.contentHtml:
Every modern state must decide how law and religion relate. International law states the principle: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) protects "freedom of thought, conscience and religion,"1 including freedom to change one's religion and to manifest it "in teaching, practice, worship and observance." Arrangements differ widely.

The United States model is disestablishment. The First Amendment (1791) bars Congress from making any law "respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof."2 It first bound only the federal government; Massachusetts kept a tax-supported church until 1833. American separation was meant partly to protect religion from the state, and public religious expression remains common. French laïcité, grounded in the 1905 law separating churches and state, grew out of conflict with the Catholic Church and stresses the neutrality of public institutions; a 2004 law bans conspicuous religious symbols in state schools. Other democracies keep established churches (the Church of England, the Danish People's Church) or cooperate with recognized religions, as Germany does by collecting church tax on their behalf. India's constitution, which added the word "secular" in 1976, pairs state neutrality with separate religious personal laws for family matters, a model the political theorist Rajeev Bhargava calls "principled distance."

Law also forces the definition problem from the first lesson. In United States v. Seeger (1965), the Supreme Court read a conscientious objector statute to cover any sincere belief that occupies in a person's life "a place parallel to that filled by the God" of traditional believers:3 a functional definition written into law.
